## Where we are

- W03 ended badly on purpose: estimating $p_{\text{data}}$ in high dimension is hopeless
- But generation never needed the density — it needed **samples**
- Today: the classical answer, and the exact point where it stops

::: {.note}
Everything this course does reduces to one request: **produce a draw from a
distribution**. Today we solve that request in the case where you can write the
target down — and find that the case we care about is not that one.
:::

## The setting

You can evaluate the target, but only up to a constant:

$$\pi(x) \;=\; \frac{\tilde\pi(x)}{Z}, \qquad Z = \int \tilde\pi(x)\,dx$$

- $\tilde\pi$ — cheap, closed form, evaluable anywhere
- $Z$ — an integral over the whole space that nobody can do

This is not a special case. It is the **generic** case.

## Three places it shows up

**Bayesian posterior**

$$p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) = \frac{p(\theta)\,L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)}{p(\mathcal{D})},
\qquad p(\mathcal{D}) = \int p(\theta) L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)\, d\theta$$

Numerator: prior × likelihood, both chosen by you. Denominator: intractable.

**Energy-based model** — $\pi(x) \propto e^{-E(x)}$, and $Z$ is the partition function

**Conditioning** — $\pi(x) \propto p(x)$ restricted to a region $A$; the mass $p(A)$ is unknown

## Why not rejection sampling?

Note 06: draw $x \sim q$, accept if $u < \pi(x)/Mq(x)$. Exact — and useless.

Target $\mathcal{N}(0,I_d)$, proposal $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_d)$: acceptance rate $\sigma^{-d}$.

| $d$ | $\sigma = 1.1$ | $\sigma = 1.5$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.91 | 0.67 |
| 10 | 0.39 | 0.017 |
| 100 | $7 \times 10^{-5}$ | $2 \times 10^{-18}$ |

::: {.note}
A proposal **ten percent** too wide is already dead at $d = 100$. Every draw is a
fresh, independent gamble against the same odds — nothing is ever learned.
:::

## The fix, in one sentence

::: {style="text-align:center"}
[Stop starting over. Move from where you already are.]{.big}
:::

A **Markov chain**: the next state depends on the past only through the present.

$$\mathbb{P}(x_{t+1} \in A \mid x_t, \dots, x_0) \;=\; \int_A K(x_t,y)\,dy$$

The kernel $K(x,y)$ is all the chain is.

## A chain is a *sequence* of distributions

Run the kernel forward from any starting law $p_0$:

$$p_{t+1}(y) \;=\; \int p_t(x)\,K(x,y)\,dx$$

There is not one distribution here — there are $p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots$ **flowing**.

::: {.note}
Note 06 computed this flow exactly for Gibbs on a bivariate normal:
$x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\rho^{2t}x_0,\; 1-\rho^{4t}\big)$.
Mean decays, variance climbs. **Burn-in** is the stretch where the flow is still
visibly incomplete.
:::

## Stationarity

$\pi$ is **stationary** for $K$ when one more step changes nothing:

$$\boxed{\;\pi(y) \;=\; \int \pi(x)\,K(x,y)\,dx\;}$$

Add **irreducibility** (can reach anywhere) and **aperiodicity** (no fixed cycle) and
the chain is ergodic: $p_t \to \pi$ from any start, and

$$\frac1T \sum_{t=1}^{T} f(x_t) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathbb{E}_\pi[f(X)]$$

## The design problem, run backwards

- Usual question: *here is a chain — what is its stationary distribution?*
- Our question: **here is the distribution — build me a chain**

::: {.note}
Checking $\pi = \pi K$ directly means an integral over the whole space, which is
the thing we are trying to avoid. We need a condition that is **local**, so it can
be engineered pointwise.
:::

## Detailed balance

A chain is **reversible** with respect to $\pi$ if for every pair of states

$$\boxed{\;\pi(x)\,K(x,y) \;=\; \pi(y)\,K(y,x)\;}$$

At equilibrium, mass flowing $x \to y$ equals mass flowing $y \to x$. Every
pairwise exchange balances.

::: {.fragment}
**It implies stationarity, in one line:**

$$\int \pi(x)K(x,y)\,dx = \int \pi(y)K(y,x)\,dx = \pi(y)\int K(y,x)\,dx = \pi(y)$$
:::

## The algorithm

Pick **any** proposal $q(y \mid x)$ you can sample from. From state $x_t$:

1. Propose $y \sim q(\cdot \mid x_t)$
2. Compute

$$\boxed{\;\alpha(x_t,y) \;=\; \min\!\left\{1,\;
\frac{\pi(y)\,q(x_t \mid y)}{\pi(x_t)\,q(y \mid x_t)}\right\}\;}$$

3. Draw $u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$: accept $x_{t+1} = y$ if $u < \alpha$,
   otherwise $x_{t+1} = x_t$

## The constant cancels

$\pi$ enters **only** through a ratio:

$$\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)} \;=\; \frac{\tilde\pi(y)/Z}{\tilde\pi(x)/Z} \;=\; \frac{\tilde\pi(y)}{\tilde\pi(x)}$$

For a Bayesian posterior with a symmetric proposal the rule is literally

$$\alpha \;=\; \min\!\left\{1,\;\frac{p(\theta')\,L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta')}{p(\theta)\,L(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)}\right\}$$

::: {.note}
Prior × likelihood at two points. **The evidence integral — the entire reason the
posterior was intractable — never appears.**
:::

## Rejection is not a discarded draw

::: {style="text-align:center"}
[A rejected proposal means the chain **emits the current state again**.]{.big}
:::

- Staying put is a legal move, and a genuine sample
- It is how the chain gives extra weight to high-density regions
- Recording only *accepted* states is the most common implementation bug — and it
  silently biases every estimate

## Why it works

For $y \ne x$ the kernel is $K(x,y) = q(y\mid x)\,\alpha(x,y)$. Push the positive
factor inside the $\min$:

$$\pi(x)\,q(y\mid x)\min\!\left\{1, \frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\right\}
= \min\big\{\pi(x)q(y\mid x),\; \pi(y)q(x\mid y)\big\}$$

::: {.fragment}
The right-hand side is **symmetric in $x \leftrightarrow y$** — swapping labels
swaps the two arguments of a $\min$ and changes nothing.

So $\pi(x)K(x,y) = \pi(y)K(y,x)$: detailed balance, hence stationarity. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.fragment}
The acceptance rule was *reverse-engineered* to make that $\min$ appear.
:::

## Random-walk Metropolis

Symmetric proposal $q(y\mid x) = \mathcal{N}(y; x, \tau^2 I)$, so the $q$-ratio is 1:

$$\alpha \;=\; \min\!\left\{1, \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi(x)}\right\}$$

- **Always** move uphill
- Move **downhill** with probability equal to the density ratio

::: {.note}
The downhill move is not a defect — it is the difference between **sampling** and
**optimisation**. A hill-climber reports the mode; a sampler must visit the tails
in proportion to their mass.
:::

## Two more special cases

**Independence sampler** — $q(y\mid x) = q(y)$, ignoring the current state.
Then $\alpha = \min\{1, w(y)/w(x)\}$ with $w = \pi/q$: accept if the candidate's
importance weight beats the incumbent's.

**Gibbs is MH with $\alpha \equiv 1$** — propose one coordinate from its exact
conditional $\pi(y_i \mid x_{-i})$; substitute into the ratio and everything
cancels.

::: {.note}
Gibbs never rejects. The price is that you must be able to sample every
conditional exactly.
:::

## MALA: the score walks in

Nothing says the proposal has to be blind. Drift toward high density *first*:

$$y \;=\; x + \tfrac{\tau^2}{2}\,\nabla_x \log \pi(x) + \tau\,z,
\qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$$

then accept/reject as usual.

::: {.note}
It needs only $\nabla_x \log \pi$ — the **score**. The normalising constant
differentiates away. Drop the accept/reject step and this is Langevin dynamics.

**This is the closest classical ancestor of a score-based generative model.**
Module 4 learns that score from data instead of deriving it.
:::

## What it costs

| | |
|---|---|
| **Burn-in** | early samples come from $p_t \ne \pi$ and are discarded |
| **Autocorrelation** | consecutive states are dependent by construction |
| **Effective sample size** | $\mathrm{ESS} = T \big/ \big(1 + 2\sum_k \rho_k\big)$ |

::: {.note}
Note 06's Gibbs example: lag-1 autocorrelation $\rho^2$. A target with $\rho =
0.99$ gives ESS about a **fiftieth** of the chain length.
:::

## Step size is a real dilemma

| $\tau$ | acceptance | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| too small | $\to 1$ | every move accepted, every move tiny — needs $\sim (L/\tau)^2$ steps to cross |
| too large | $\to 0$ | proposals land in the tails; the chain sticks for hundreds of steps |
| tuned | $\approx 0.234$ | the asymptotically optimal rate (Roberts, Gelman & Gilks, 1997) |

::: {.note}
The beginner's instinct — *"95% acceptance, it must be working"* — is exactly
backwards. It almost always means the chain is crawling.
:::

## And the curse, once more

Steps needed per **independent** sample, for product-form targets:

| sampler | scaling |
|---|---|
| random-walk Metropolis | $O(d)$ |
| MALA (adjusted Langevin) | $O(d^{1/3})$ |
| Hamiltonian Monte Carlo | $O(d^{1/4})$ |

::: {.note}
Against rejection sampling's $\sigma^{-d}$ this is a triumph — polynomial, not
exponential. Against $d \approx 10^5$ for a modest image, it is still nowhere
near enough.
:::

## The failure that hides best

A chain in one mode of a well-separated bimodal target must cross a low-density
valley. The probability of proposing across it can be $e^{-100}$.

The chain then looks **perfectly healthy**:

- good acceptance rate
- stable trace plot
- tight autocorrelation

::: {.note}
It has converged — to a **mode**, not to $\pi$. Tempering, parallel chains and
mode-hopping proposals help; none is a general solution. Remember this slide when
we meet mode collapse in Part 2.
:::

## Now suppose every difficulty were solved

Perfect tuning. No multimodality. Dimension-free mixing.

::: {.fragment}
**It still cannot generate an image.** The obstruction is not efficiency — it is
the *input*.
:::

::: {.fragment}
MH answers:

> *"I can write the target down up to a constant. Give me samples."*

Generative modelling asks:

> *"I cannot write it down at all. I have 60,000 samples. Give me more."*
:::

## There is no $\tilde\pi$ for images

- Nobody can supply a function that takes a $256\times256\times3$ array and
  returns a number proportional to how likely it is to be a photograph
- That function is precisely what W03 proved we cannot estimate
- **MH converts a density into samples — and we have no density to feed it**

::: {.fragment}
And MH never *learns*. A million steps, then a fresh start, and you pay the full
burn-in again. Nothing is trained, nothing amortised.
:::

## The pivot

In rejection sampling, in MH, in Gibbs — **a human picks the proposal for
convenience and hopes it resembles the target.** In high dimension it does not.

::: {style="text-align:center"}
[So stop picking it. **Learn** it.]{.big}
:::

::: {.note}
Which immediately raises the question that defines Part 2: if you never evaluate a
density, **how do you know your generator is any good?** You cannot compute a
likelihood, so you cannot maximise one.
:::
